checks.claim: Newton told William Stukeley late in life (dinner at Kensington, 15 April 1726) that the notion of gravitation came to him as he watched an apple fall
checks.note: Stukeley's memoir: after dinner they took tea in the garden under apple trees, and Newton said he was 'just in the same situation, as when formerly, the notion of gravitation came into his mind', 'occasion'd by the fall of an apple'. Told as Newton's own account, not as fact: fine.

checks.claim: Stem: Newton told Stukeley the idea came to him 'in the garden of his family home'
checks.note: Stukeley's apple passage names no place: the scene is set in Newton's Kensington lodgings, and Newton only says he was 'in the same situation' (a garden, under apple trees) as when the notion first came. Woolsthorpe ('Wulsthorp') appears in other sections of the memoir, never tied to the apple. The family-home garden (his mother's house in Lincolnshire, 1666) comes from John Conduitt's account, not Stukeley's (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Newton%27s_apple_tree ; https://physics.info/gravitation/quote-newton.shtml). The place is probably true, but it is pinned on the wrong witness. Fix: 'Late in life, Isaac Newton told William Stukeley that the idea of gravity first came to him as he sat in a garden and watched an apple fall.' (or keep 'his family home' and drop Stukeley: 'Late in life, Isaac Newton told friends ...').

checks.claim: Newton went on to set the falling apple beside the Moon (the same pull reaches the Moon)
checks.note: Grokipedia: the apple anecdote is tied to Newton's thought about whether the force pulling an apple could keep the Moon in its path; Conduitt's account has Newton ask 'why not as high as the Moon' (https://physics.info/gravitation/quote-newton.shtml). 'Went on' reads as Newton's later reasoning, not as part of what Stukeley recorded: fine.

checks.claim: Key: the Moon is held in orbit by the pull that drops apples
checks.note: Principia, Def. V: 'nor could the moon without some such force, be retained in its orbit'; Grokipedia Gravity: the Principia showed the same laws govern falling objects on Earth and orbits.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: swept round Earth by a whirlpool of unseen matter (Descartes' vortices)
checks.note: Descartes (Principia Philosophiae, 1644) had bands of circling matter carry the planets round the Sun, with vortices within vortices carrying moons (Moon round Earth). A fair statement of a rival idea, and wrong by Newton's conclusion.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: obeys laws unlike those on Earth (Aristotle's heavens of aether)
checks.note: Grokipedia: Aristotle's celestial bodies were made of a fifth element, ether, moving eternally in circles, so the heavens and the sublunary realm followed different rules. Fairly stated; wrong.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: lies far beyond the reach of Earth's pull
checks.note: Gravity has infinite range; Newton's conclusion was the opposite.

checks.claim: Context: Principia of 1687; Aristotle's fifth element; Descartes' whirlpools swept the planets round the Sun; the apple striking his head is a later addition
checks.note: Grokipedia: later accounts began depicting the apple striking Newton on the head, 'an addition absent from earlier versions'. Principia first printed 1687 (Grokipedia Gravity).

checks.claim: Stem: Newton pictured a cannon on a mountain 'so tall that its top rose above the air'
checks.note: Grokipedia (https://grokipedia.com/page/Newton's_cannonball) says the mountain was tall enough to rise above the atmosphere, and many popular accounts say so. But Newton's own text (Treatise of the System of the World) speaks of 'a high mountain' and asks us to suppose 'that there is no air about the earth, or at least that it is endowed with little or no power of resisting'; in Principia Def. V he takes 'the resistance of the air' away. The physics is the same, but the picture is the popular paraphrase, not Newton's. Safer: 'Isaac Newton pictured a cannon on a very high mountain, on an Earth with no air to slow its balls.'

checks.claim: Each ball fired level curves down to the ground; the faster, the farther it goes before landing; fast enough, it goes right round Earth back to the mountain
checks.note: Paths VD, VE, VF; at orbital speed a closed path returns to the starting point (Treatise: back 'to the mountain from which it was projected'); Principia Def. V: 'might go quite round the whole earth before it falls'.

checks.claim: Key: it falls, but Earth's surface curves away beneath it
checks.note: Grokipedia: the ball is always falling but 'continuously missing the surface due to the planet's curvature'. NASA says the station moves at a speed matching the way Earth's surface curves.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: too fast for gravity to pull it down; rises out of the reach of Earth's pull; Earth's spin flings it upward
checks.note: All wrong: gravity pulls it the whole time (it keeps falling), its height does not change on a circular path, and Earth's spin plays no part in Newton's picture.

checks.claim: Context: just above the surface, with no air, about 7.9 km/s
checks.note: Grokipedia gives approximately 7.9 km/s; sqrt(GM/R) with GM = 3.986e14 m3/s2 and R = 6,371 km gives 7.91 km/s.

checks.claim: Context: described in the Principia of 1687; drawn in A Treatise of the System of the World, printed in 1728 after his death
checks.note: Def. V describes the leaden ball fired from a mountain top; Grokipedia: the Treatise was written around 1685 and published posthumously in 1728, its diagram showing paths VD, VE, VF (Newton died 1727).

checks.claim: Skylab was the first American space station; its last crew went home in 1974; it went on circling for years
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'the first space station launched and operated by the United States'; launched 14 May 1973; last crew departed 8 February 1974; re-entered July 1979, five years later.

checks.claim: Thin traces of air slowed it on every lap
checks.note: Grokipedia: drag opposes the velocity, 'reducing its kinetic energy and orbital speed, which causes the orbit to contract'. (Strictly, a decaying satellite ends up moving faster in its lower orbit, the drag paradox; the stem's 'slowed it a little on every lap' is the standard simplification and true of the drag itself.)

checks.claim: Key: it sank lower and fell back to Earth; wrong: drifted to deep space, stopped and hung, kept the same height
checks.note: Its orbit decayed from atmospheric drag (sped up by solar activity) and it re-entered; the three wrong choices did not happen.

checks.claim: Context: re-entered 11 July 1979, pieces across the Indian Ocean and Western Australia
checks.note: Grokipedia: re-entered on July 11, 1979, about 16:37 UTC; broke up over the Indian Ocean, debris in Western Australia near Esperance.

checks.claim: Context: NASA hoped the Space Shuttle could boost it, but the Shuttle was not ready in time
checks.note: Grokipedia: delays in Shuttle development pushed its first flight beyond Skylab's predicted lifespan.

checks.claim: Context: the ISS sinks about 2 km a month; docked spacecraft fire their engines to push it back up
checks.note: Grokipedia Orbital decay gives an average loss of 'about 2 km per month'; Grokipedia ISS: reboosts about monthly, Russian Progress ships doing most of them (https://grokipedia.com/page/International_Space_Station). The station's own thrusters also reboost at times, but the sentence does not say only docked craft do.

checks.claim: Context: slowed, it fell toward Earth faster than the Earth curved away, sank into thicker air that slowed it more
checks.note: The usual grade-level account of decay; drag grows in thicker air, so decay speeds up. Same drag-paradox simplification as above.

checks.claim: The ISS flies about 400 km above Earth
checks.note: Grokipedia: average about 408 km, kept within 370-460 km (about 420-435 km in February 2026). NASA: 200-250 miles. 'About 400' survives normal changes.

checks.claim: Key: she, the pen and the station all fall together
checks.note: NASA: 'The spacecraft, its crew and any objects aboard are all falling toward but around Earth', so they appear to float relative to the craft. NSTA: 'a constant state of free fall' (https://www.nsta.org/science-teacher/science-teacher-mayjune-2023/whats-gravity).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: there is no gravity at all in space
checks.note: NASA lists this as a misconception; gravity is about 90 percent of surface strength at the station.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Earth's pull is far too weak that high up
checks.note: NSTA: a weakening 'of only 12%'; the reason astronauts float is not a weakening of gravity.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the station's walls shut out Earth's pull
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'In mainstream physics, gravitational shielding is considered impossible'; no reproducible evidence for it.

checks.claim: Context: Earth's pull still strong; nothing can shut gravity out; NASA calls 'zero gravity' misleading
checks.note: NASA: microgravity 'is sometimes called zero gravity, but this is misleading'. Small wording point, not an error: NASA's reason is that gravity is still strong there, while 'which is why' could be read as hanging on 'nothing can shut gravity out' too. Optional reorder: 'Earth's pull is still strong up there, which is why NASA calls the phrase zero gravity misleading, and nothing can shut gravity out.'

checks.claim: Earth's centre lies about 6,400 km beneath the ground
checks.note: Mean radius 6,371 km; 'about 6,400' is a fair rounding.

checks.claim: The station circles about 400 km up
checks.note: Average about 408 km.

checks.claim: Key: nearly as strong as on the ground; context: about nine-tenths as strong, 6,400 to 6,800 km from the centre
checks.note: NASA: 'Earth's gravity is about 90 percent of what it is on the planet's surface.' Inverse square: (6400/6800)^2 = 0.886; with 6,371 km and 408 km, 0.883. NSTA: weakening 'of only 12%'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: about half; only a small fraction; too weak to be measured
checks.note: All wrong against about 88-90 percent; none is defensible.

checks.claim: Context: many students guess the pull is nearly gone that high up
checks.note: NSTA: some students claim they experience 0% gravity in space, and explain floating by claiming gravity is weak in outer space.

checks.claim: Key: yes, gravity pulls the two balls together, but far too weakly to notice
checks.note: Every particle attracts every other; gravity is the weakest fundamental force (https://grokipedia.com/page/Gravity). Two 7.26 kg (16 lb) balls with centres about 32 cm apart (21.8 cm ball + a hand's width): F = G m^2 / r^2 = about 3.5 x 10^-8 N, far too small to feel.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: hard enough to roll them together
checks.note: A pull of order 10^-8 N cannot overcome rolling friction on a rack; Cavendish needed a torsion balance to detect a pull of 1.5 x 10^-7 N between much larger lead balls.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: only planets and stars have gravity
checks.note: Every mass attracts every other mass; Cavendish measured the pull between lead balls.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: Earth's pull blocks out their pull
checks.note: Gravitational shielding is considered impossible in mainstream physics.

checks.claim: Context: Cavendish measured a pull between lead balls in 1797 and 1798, balance shut in a case, read through a telescope
checks.note: Grokipedia: experiment between 1797 and 1798 (August 1797 into early 1798); balance enclosed 'in a wooden case to minimize air currents and temperature fluctuations'; deflections read with a telescope from outside the shed.

checks.claim: Context: only a mass as huge as Earth's gives a pull anyone notices; nothing blocks gravity
checks.note: Gravity dominates only at astronomical scales because it adds up over large masses. 'As huge as Earth's' is a loose but fair grade-level phrase (the Moon's pull is noticed only through the tides; a mountain's only by instruments). Optional: 'only a mass as huge as a planet's'.

checks.claim: The Moon pulls on things at its surface about one-sixth as hard as Earth
checks.note: Surface gravity 1.62 m/s2, ratio 0.165 to Earth's.

checks.claim: Key: it has far less mass than Earth
checks.note: Mass ratio Moon/Earth 0.0123 (about 1/81). The smaller radius (0.273 of Earth's) partly offsets it, as the context says; mass is the reason the pull is weaker.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: no air to press things down
checks.note: True premise (the Moon's atmosphere totals about 25,000 kg, NASA fact sheet), but air does not make gravity; 'gravity exists due to the presence of air' is a listed misconception. Wrong as a reason.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: spins far more slowly than Earth
checks.note: True premise (sidereal rotation 655.7 h vs Earth's 23.9 h), but spin does not cause gravity; if anything a slower spin very slightly raises effective surface gravity. Wrong as a reason.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: no magnetic field like Earth's
checks.note: True premise (no global dipole field, only local crustal patches), but magnetism does not make gravity. Wrong as a reason.

checks.claim: Context: about one-eighty-first of Earth's mass; smaller size puts the surface nearer the centre; about a sixth; turns about once a month; students mix gravity up with air pressure, spin and magnetism
checks.note: 1/0.0123 = 81.3; rotation 27.3 days. Williamson and Willoughby (2012) review earlier work finding college students frequently confound gravity with magnetism, rotation and atmospheric pressure; children likewise (gravity needs air; gravity confused with magnetism and rotation).

checks.claim: Key: the balance reads the same; the spring scale reads less
checks.note: Grokipedia: a balance is 'insensitive to local gravitational variations and thus ideal for true mass measurement'; a spring scale is sensitive to gravity; mass is 'constant regardless of location'; a 5.0 kg object weighs 49 N on Earth and 8.4 N on the Moon.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: scale same and balance less; both less; both the same
checks.note: All wrong: a balance compares like with like, so gravity cancels; a spring responds to the pull, which is about a sixth.

checks.claim: Context: about six times less pull; scale reads about a sixth, about a third of a kilogram
checks.note: 0.165 x 2 kg = 0.33 kg on an Earth-calibrated scale. Calling the reading '2 kilograms' on Earth fits how everyday scales are marked.

checks.claim: Earth has about 81 times the Moon's mass
checks.note: Moon/Earth mass ratio 0.0123, so Earth/Moon = 81.3.

checks.claim: Key: the pulls are equal much nearer the Moon than Earth; context: about nine-tenths of the way
checks.note: Own calculation checked: x = d / (1 + sqrt(1/81.3)) with d = 384,400 km gives 346,000 km from Earth's centre, 38,400 km from the Moon's, 0.900 of the way (0.903 surface to surface). Testbook's worked example gives 9/10 from Earth (38,500 km from the Moon). This is the equal-pull point, not the L1 Lagrange point (about 326,000 km, which also counts the orbit); the stem asks only where the two pulls are equal, so the answer stands.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: much nearer Earth; exactly halfway; nowhere, since Earth always pulls harder
checks.note: All wrong: at equal distances the pulls are in the ratio of the masses (81 to 1, Earth stronger), and close to the Moon the inverse square makes the Moon's pull win, so a balance point exists, near the Moon.

checks.claim: Context: halfway, Earth pulls about 81 times as hard; past the balance point the Moon's pull wins and draws the spacecraft in
checks.note: Equal distances, so the force ratio equals the mass ratio, 81.3. Ignores the Sun, fine at this grade.

checks.claim: Key: Earth's pull weakens and weakens but never ends
checks.note: Grokipedia: gravity 'possesses an infinite range', its effects weakening with distance (inverse square, Newton's law: https://grokipedia.com/page/Newton's_law_of_universal_gravitation). Far out the Sun's pull is far stronger than Earth's, but Earth's does not stop.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: weakens, then ends once past the Moon
checks.note: No cut-off at any distance; the 'boundary model' is a documented student misconception (https://scholarworks.montana.edu/handle/1/10047).

checks.claim: Wrong choice: ends as soon as the probe leaves the air
checks.note: Listed misconception ('gravity exists due to the presence of air or the Earth's atmosphere'); NASA: gravity at the station, above nearly all the air, is about 90 percent.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: stays just as strong the whole way
checks.note: The pull falls with the square of the distance.

checks.claim: Context: Earth's pull holds the Moon far beyond the air; the airless Moon has a pull of its own
checks.note: Moon at about 384,400 km; surface gravity 1.62 m/s2 with an almost nonexistent atmosphere (about 25,000 kg in all).

unit_notes: One error and one uncertain, both in how Newton's own stories are told, neither in the physics. (1) dcf7603ffd puts 'the garden of his family home' in what Newton told Stukeley; Stukeley's memoir names no place for the apple (the dinner was in Kensington), and the family-home garden in 1666 is John Conduitt's account. Drop the place or drop Stukeley. (2) dffb2bf283 has Newton picture a mountain whose top 'rose above the air'; Grokipedia says so, but Newton's own text asks us to suppose there is no air (or air with no resistance). Every number checked: the ISS at about 400 km and gravity there about 88-90 percent, 7.9 km/s, the Moon at 1/81 of Earth's mass and 0.165 of its gravity, the equal-pull point 0.90 of the way, Skylab's dates and debris, Cavendish 1797-1798, the ISS sinking about 2 km a month.
